solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Second best's hilarious

definitions.note: the answer as an informal noun, something very funny; 'it was hilarious' becomes 'it was a laugh'

parts.note: the cream is the best part of anything, as in the cream of the crop

explanation.surface: Someone declares that the runner-up's performance was very funny.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's after 'best' stands for 'is' and links wordplay to definition. Strictly the answer is a noun (a laugh), so the swap needs 'a' before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling something a laugh riot or a real howler is the informal noun sense of very funny.

clue.text: Alluring woman is upset about note

indicators.note: upset means turned over, so in a down entry the two letters are read upwards

parts.note: re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: A seductive woman becomes upset over a written message.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns IS into SI. 'Note' looks like a musical or written message but just gives N.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the Sirens lured sailors with song, so a seductive temptress is one.

clue.text: Two contrasting organs' endless piano music

parts.note: organs are newspapers; a rag is a disreputable paper

indicators.note: endless means losing the final letter of the paper's name

parts.note: The Times is a heavyweight British newspaper, the opposite of a rag

explanation.surface: Two very different body parts provide endless keyboard music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'organs' are newspapers, not body parts: a rag (a scandal sheet) and The Times. 'endless' drops the S from TIMES.
explanation.definitionFit: Ragtime is the syncopated American piano style made famous by Scott Joplin.

clue.text: Spanish region, also a large one in the States

parts.note: and means also, in addition
L is the standard abbreviation for large, as on clothing sizes

indicators.note: in places the numeral inside the abbreviation for America

parts.note: USA stands for the United States of America
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: There is a Spanish region and also a big one in America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is the container signal here, not a link; 'a large one' reads like a big region but splits into A, L and the numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: Andalusia is the autonomous community covering southern Spain, home to Seville and Granada.

clue.text: Woeful first aid is struck off course

indicators.note: woeful means pitifully bad, suggesting the letters are in a sorry, jumbled state
struck off means removed, so these two letters are deleted from the pool

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to be trimmed and shuffled
taken as written

explanation.surface: Poor emergency treatment gets someone struck off the medical register.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is struck' removes an I and the S from FIRST AID, leaving FRTAID, which 'Woeful' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: A boat drifting without control or direction has gone off course.

clue.text: Leave old road going up to see Burgess' Russian "friend"

indicators.note: in a down entry going up means the letters are read from bottom to top

parts.note: to go is to leave

explanation.surface: Someone walks off the old road to visit Burgess's Russian pal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going up' reverses GO-O-RD. In Anthony Burgess's novel A Clockwork Orange, the Russian-based slang Nadsat calls a gang member a droog, from Russian drug, friend.
explanation.definitionFit: A droog is a friend or gang mate in the invented teen slang of A Clockwork Orange.

clue.text: Thorough training of pathfinder may get you this far

indicators.note: training suggests the letters are drilled and reformed into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written: the letters to be rearranged
taken as written: the letters left over once the answer is formed

explanation.surface: A scout's thorough instruction will take you a long way.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite: rearrange PATHFINDER as the answer plus FAR, so the answer is PATHFINDER less the letters of 'far'. 'may get you this' links them.
explanation.definitionFit: An in-depth study is detailed and comprehensive, which is what thorough means.

clue.text: Split up police seizing new office equipment

indicators.note: in a down entry up means the word is read upwards

parts.note: to part is to split or separate

indicators.note: seizing means grabbing hold of, so the slang word encloses the letter

parts.note: pigs is a derogatory slang term for the police

explanation.surface: Police raid a business and seize the new office equipment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns the split word upwards and 'seizing' wraps the slang word round N. 'Office' means a post held, whose trappings are its outward symbols, not desks and staplers.
explanation.definitionFit: The trappings of office are the outward signs and accessories that come with holding a post.

clue.text: Go over old sad event

indicators.note: over means covering or around, so the attempt surrounds the other piece

parts.note: a go is an attempt, a try
aged means old

explanation.surface: Someone recalls a past misfortune by going over it again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go over' reads as one verb, revisit, but 'over' is the container signal wrapping the attempt round the word for old.
explanation.definitionFit: A tragedy is a disastrous or deeply sorrowful happening.

clue.text: Duty men return, a tad frustrated and cross

indicators.note: return means go back, so the two letters for men are read backwards

parts.note: OR (other ranks) is the crossword abbreviation for soldiers who are not officers

indicators.note: frustrated suggests the letters are thwarted and thrown out of order

parts.note: taken as written for the shuffle
X is the shape of a cross

explanation.surface: Annoyed workers come back slightly irritated and angry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return' turns OR into RO; 'frustrated' scrambles A TAD into ADTA. Road tax is the UK annual charge on keeping a vehicle on public roads.
explanation.definitionFit: A duty is a tax levied by the state, here the charge on owning a car.

clue.text: Elect Euro politicians tackling top- class medicines

parts.note: to elect is to pick or choose

indicators.note: tackling means grappling with, so the politicians grip the letter inside

parts.note: MEPs are Members of the European Parliament
U means upper-class, the top class in British social shorthand

explanation.surface: Voters choose European politicians who tackle top-quality drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tackling' puts U inside MEPS. U for upper class comes from a famous 1950s British essay on 'U and non-U' speech.
explanation.definitionFit: A pick-me-up is a tonic or drink taken to restore energy, a kind of medicine.

clue.text: Indulge in trips round Yankee firm

indicators.note: round means surrounding, so the shuffled letters go around the single letter
trips means stumbles, so these letters fall over into a new order

parts.note: taken as written for the shuffle
taken as written for the shuffle
Yankee is Y in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone is urged to treat themselves to journeys around America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trips' scrambles the fodder into UNIELDING, and 'round' wraps that around Y after the N. 'in' looks like a link but is part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone firm in their position will not bend or give way.

clue.text: US writer holds page for poet

indicators.note: holds means contains, so the writer's name has the page inside it

parts.note: Edgar Allan Poe was an American author

explanation.surface: An American author keeps hold of a page meant for a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holds' puts P inside POE. Alexander Pope was an English poet, so one writer's name hides inside another's.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexander Pope, author of The Rape of the Lock, is a celebrated English poet.

clue.text: Not all quaff retsina in little bars

indicators.note: Not all says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone drinks only part of the Greek wine in small pubs.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is 'little bars' alone, with 'in' as a link: frets are the small ridges on a guitar neck; the draft's 'in little bars' would not substitute for the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Frets are the thin raised strips across a guitar's fingerboard, small metal bars.

clue.text: Stroke loosens part of roof, say

parts.note: to free something is to loosen it

indicators.note: say signals that the roof word is to be heard rather than spelt

parts.note: a tile is one piece of a roof covering

explanation.surface: A stroke dislodges part of a roof, as it were.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' gives TYLE, which is pronounced like TILE. 'Stroke' looks like a blow but is the swimming style.
explanation.definitionFit: Freestyle is the swimming race where any stroke is allowed, in practice the front crawl.

clue.text: Aberdonian knows about long galleys

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the Scots word wraps around the other piece

parts.note: ken is Scots for know, so a Scot from Aberdeen kens
to long for something is to itch for it

explanation.surface: A man from Aberdeen is familiar with long ship's kitchens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' is the container signal. Aberdeen is a city in Scotland, where 'ken' means know; 'long' looks like an adjective for galleys but is the verb to yearn.
explanation.definitionFit: A galley is the cooking area on a ship or aircraft.

clue.text: Blair concealed controversial items in evidence

indicators.note: concealed means hid inside, so the first name surrounds the shuffled letters

parts.note: Tony Blair was the UK prime minister from 1997 to 2007

indicators.note: controversial suggests the letters are disputed and thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written for the shuffle

explanation.surface: A former prime minister hid contentious items that were evidence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'controversial' reorders the five letters of 'items' as ESTIM; 'concealed' hides them in the former prime minister's first name, after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Testimony is evidence given by a witness, usually under oath in court.

clue.text: Slug left hole in one decorative band

parts.note: to slug a drink is to neck it, gulp it down
in golf a hole in one is called an ace

explanation.surface: A slug crawled away and left a hole in a decorative band.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slug' looks like the garden pest but is a verb, to gulp a drink, which is also NECK in British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: A necklace is an ornamental chain or string of beads worn around the neck.

clue.text: Lily leaves behind Caribbean isle's TV controllers

indicators.note: behind means placed after, so the leaves come after the island

parts.note: a key or cay is a low island in the Caribbean, like Key West
lily pads are the floating leaves of water lilies

explanation.surface: A water lily drops its leaves behind on a Caribbean island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaves' looks like a verb, departs, but pairs with 'Lily' to give PADS.
explanation.definitionFit: Keypads are the button panels on remote controls used to operate a television.

clue.text: Small prize money cut incentives

indicators.note: cut means shortened, so the last letter of the prize word is lopped off

parts.note: a purse is the prize money in a boxing match or race

explanation.surface: A reduction in modest prize money takes away the motivation to compete.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut' docks the final E from PURSE, leaving PURS.
explanation.definitionFit: Spurs are things that urge someone on, like the riders' spikes that drive a horse forward.

clue.text: Promote film ratings and read novel

parts.note: U (universal) is a British film classification suitable for all
PG (parental guidance) is another film certificate

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters are given a new order

parts.note: taken as written for the shuffle

explanation.surface: Someone advertises film certificates and reads a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like a book to read but means new, rearranging READ to RADE.
explanation.definitionFit: To upgrade someone is to raise them to a higher grade or rank.

clue.text: Spot cryptic clue for Burgess?

definitions.meaning: to spot is to catch sight of
split after its first letter, the word becomes a mini clue, English spy, describing Guy Burgess

explanation.walkthrough: Guy Burgess was an English diplomat who spied for the Soviet Union; split the answer as E (English) plus SPY and it describes him.
explanation.definitionFit: To espy is to catch sight of, an old-fashioned way of saying notice.

clue.text: No-frills shopping made in high dudgeon

indicators.note: frills are the edges of a garment, so the phrase loses its outside letters and the rest sits within it

explanation.surface: A bargain shopping trip leaves someone furious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No-frills' strips the first S and last E from the phrase SHOPPING MADE, leaving the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Hopping mad is an idiom for extremely angry, just as in high dudgeon is.

clue.text: Stolen article from 3 stays here

definitions.note: a place where someone stays, said of the answer as a noun

parts.note: hot is slang for stolen goods
3 is a Spanish region, and el is the Spanish definite article

explanation.surface: A stolen item from Andalusia is kept here.
explanation.walkthrough: The '3' sends you to 3-down, a Spanish region, so the article is Spanish EL. The definition is a loose description: a traveller stays here.
explanation.definitionFit: A hotel is an establishment where travellers pay to stay the night.

clue.text: American sailors take care of mast

indicators.note: take means accept inside, so the letters for American and sailors take in the other piece

parts.note: RN is the Royal Navy, the British navy's sailors
c/o, written CO, is the postal abbreviation for care of

explanation.surface: US sailors take responsibility for looking after a ship's mast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'take' puts CO inside ARN. 'Mast' looks like part of a ship but is the fallen nuts of forest trees such as oak and beech.
explanation.definitionFit: Mast is the collective name for the nuts of oak and beech, of which an oak nut is one.

clue.text: Extremely dirty and unpleasant TV series

indicators.note: extremely points to the extremities, the first and last letters of the word

parts.note: nasty means unpleasant

explanation.surface: A television show is described as very filthy and disagreeable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' takes D and Y from 'dirty'. Dynasty was an American TV soap of the 1980s.
explanation.definitionFit: Dynasty was a long-running American prime-time soap opera about an oil family.

clue.text: Nice novel, very old, recalled one of 23

definitions.note: 23 is DYNASTY, so a member of a royal house

parts.note: roman is the French for novel, as spoken in Nice

indicators.note: recalled means called back, so the two letters are read backwards

explanation.surface: A pleasant novel, very old, is remembered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nice' looks like 'pleasant' but is the French city, so its 'novel' is ROMAN; 'recalled' turns VO into OV. The Romanovs ruled Russia until 1917.
explanation.definitionFit: The Romanovs were the dynasty of tsars who ruled Russia for three centuries.

clue.text: Midshipman drinks one litre, no problem

indicators.note: drinks means takes in, so the naval name contains the other letters

parts.note: Mr Midshipman Easy is the hero of Frederick Marryat's 1836 sea novel
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A young naval officer downs a litre of something without difficulty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drinks' puts I and L inside EASY. Mr Midshipman Easy is a classic English naval adventure novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something with no problem means doing it without effort or difficulty.

clue.text: Heraldic device with very strange name

indicators.note: strange suggests the letters are made odd by being rearranged

parts.note: taken as written for the shuffle

explanation.surface: A coat of arms bears a very odd title.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strange' reorders the fodder into YVER, which sits between the two single letters. 'device' here is a heraldic charge, not a gadget.
explanation.definitionFit: A wyvern is a two-legged winged dragon used as a charge on coats of arms.
